statement: In a mixed even p-spin [spin glass](c:spin-glass), the [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) term $H_p$ concentrates under the random [Gibbs measure](c:gibbs-measure), and if $\beta_p \ne 0$ the overlaps satisfy the Ghirlanda-Guerra identities $\mathbb{E}\langle f R_{1,n+1}^p\rangle \approx \frac1n\mathbb{E}\langle f\rangle\mathbb{E}\langle R_{1,2}^p\rangle + \frac1n\sum_{l=2}^n \mathbb{E}\langle f R_{1,l}^p\rangle$.

hypotheses.text: The Hamiltonian is a mixed p-spin [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process) with terms only for $p = 1$ and even $p \ge 2$, and its free energy converges to the Parisi formula.
The coefficient $\beta_p$ of the power $p$ in the identities is not zero.

conclusion: $\frac1N\mathbb{E}\langle|H_p(\sigma) - \mathbb{E}\langle H_p(\sigma)\rangle|\rangle \to 0$, and for $\beta_p \ne 0$, every $n \ge 2$ and every $f$ with values in $[-1,1]$, $\mathbb{E}\langle f R_{1,n+1}^p\rangle - \frac1n\mathbb{E}\langle f\rangle\mathbb{E}\langle R_{1,2}^p\rangle - \frac1n\sum_{l=2}^n\mathbb{E}\langle f R_{1,l}^p\rangle \to 0$.

proofs.name: Convexity of the free energy and integration by parts
proofs.slogan: Differentiability of the limit free energy forces the Hamiltonian to concentrate, and integration by parts turns concentration into overlap identities.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1 in Panchenko (2010), with the results of Chatterjee and Talagrand cited by the source.

roles.why: Talagrand's Parisi formula gives a differentiable limit of the [convex](c:convex-function) free energy, which controls the variance of $H_p$.
Integration by parts produces the factor $\beta_p$, so one can divide by it only if it is not zero.

steps.slogan: Split the fluctuation of $H_p$ into disorder and thermal parts.
steps.detail: The derivatives $F_N' = N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\langle H_p\rangle$ and $F_N'' = N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\langle(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle)^2\rangle$ make $F_N$ convex, and the disorder part follows from the self-averaging of the free energy.

steps.slogan: Bound the thermal fluctuation by the growth of $F_N'$ on a short interval.
steps.detail: Integration in the coefficient over $[\beta_p, \beta_p+\delta]$ and Cauchy-Schwarz give $N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\langle|H_p - \langle H_p\rangle|\rangle \le 2(\Delta_N/(N\delta))^{1/2} + 8\Delta_N$ with $\Delta_N = F_N'(\beta_p+\delta) - F_N'(\beta_p)$.

steps.slogan: Use convexity and the differentiable Parisi limit to make $\Delta_N$ small.
steps.detail: Convexity bounds $\Delta_N$ by difference quotients of $F_N$, these converge to difference quotients of the Parisi formula $P$, and differentiability of $P$ in $\beta_p$ sends the bound to $0$.

steps.slogan: Turn the concentration of $H_p$ into the overlap identities by Gaussian integration by parts.
steps.detail: With covariance $N R_{1,l}^p$, integration by parts writes $N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\langle f H_p(\sigma^1)\rangle - N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\langle f\rangle\mathbb{E}\langle H_p\rangle$ as $-n\beta_p$ times the bracket of the identities.

new_concepts.name: free energy
new_concepts.reminder: The free energy is $-1/\beta$ times the pressure $\psi=\lim|\Lambda|^{-1}\log Z_\Lambda$ of a lattice model.
new_concepts.definition: For a lattice spin model with [partition function](c:partition-function) $Z_\Lambda(\beta)$ in a finite box $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, the pressure is the [thermodynamic limit](c:thermodynamic-limit) $\psi(\beta)=\lim_{\Lambda\uparrow\mathbb Z^d}|\Lambda|^{-1}\log Z_\Lambda(\beta)$. For finite-range interactions, the limit exists along boxes, it does not depend on the boundary condition, and $\psi$ is convex.

new_concepts.name: Gibbs measure
new_concepts.reminder: A Gibbs measure is an infinite-volume law whose conditional law in each finite box is the finite Gibbs distribution.
new_concepts.definition: For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and a [boundary condition](c:boundary-condition) $\eta$, let $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ be the finite-volume [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) of an interaction in $\Lambda$, with the spins outside $\Lambda$ fixed to $\eta$. A [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ on the configuration space $S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ is a Gibbs measure if, for every finite $\Lambda$, the [conditional distribution](c:conditional-distribution) of the spins in $\Lambda$ given the spins outside $\Lambda$ is $\pi_\Lambda^\eta$ for $\mu$-almost every outside configuration $\eta$. These conditions are the DLR equations.

new_concepts.name: inverse temperature
new_concepts.reminder: The inverse temperature $\beta=1/(k_BT)$ multiplies the energy in the Boltzmann weight $e^{-\beta H}$.
new_concepts.definition: The inverse temperature of a system at absolute temperature $T$ is $\beta=1/(k_BT)$, where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. It is the parameter in the [Boltzmann distribution](c:boltzmann-distribution) $\mu_\beta(\sigma)=e^{-\beta H(\sigma)}/Z(\beta)$ of a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H$. Mathematical texts usually set $k_B=1$ and use $\beta\in[0,\infty)$ as the parameter.

new_concepts.name: spin glass
new_concepts.reminder: A spin glass is a spin system whose couplings are random and take both signs, which causes frustration.
new_concepts.definition: A spin glass is a spin system with a random Hamiltonian such as $H_J(\sigma)=-\sum_{x\sim y}J_{xy}\sigma_x\sigma_y$, where the couplings $J_{xy}$ are [iid](c:iid-random-variables) random variables with a symmetric law, for example $N(0,1)$ or $\pm1$ with equal probability. For a fixed realization of $J$, one studies the random [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) $e^{-\beta H_J(\sigma)}/Z_J$. The main quantity is the quenched [free energy](c:free-energy), built from $\mathbb E\log Z_J$.

statement: For the [Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model](c:sherrington-kirkpatrick-model) and even p-spin [spin glasses](c:spin-glass), the pressure $P_N = N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\log Z_N$ is at most the cavity functional $G_M$ of every random overlap structure, and $\lim_N P_N = \lim_M \inf G_M$, a variational formula for the [free energy](c:free-energy).

hypotheses.text: The Hamiltonian $K_N$ is a centered [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process) with $\mathbb{E}K_N(\sigma)K_N(\sigma') = \frac N2 f(q_{\sigma,\sigma'})$ and independent standard Gaussian couplings.
The mixture $f(q) = \sum_r a_r^2 q^r$ with $\sum_r a_r^2 = 1$ is [convex](c:convex-function) on $[-1,1]$.

conclusion: $P_M \le \inf_{\text{ROSt}} G_M$ for every $M$, and $\lim_{N\to\infty} P_N = \lim_{M\to\infty}\inf_{\text{ROSt}} G_M$.

proofs.name: Interpolation upper bound and cavity lower bound
proofs.slogan: Interpolate between M free spins and M spins coupled to a reservoir, then add M spins to a large system.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1 in Aizenman, Sims and Starr (2003), with the superadditivity of Guerra and Toninelli.

roles.why: Gaussian couplings allow integration by parts and the exact splitting of the Hamiltonian of $N+M$ spins into a reservoir part and cavity fields.
Convexity of $f$ makes the derivative of the interpolation nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Attach Gaussian cavity fields to the points of a random overlap structure.
steps.detail: The fields $\eta_{j,\alpha}$ and $\kappa_\alpha$ have covariances $\frac12 f'(\tilde q)$ and $\tilde q f'(\tilde q) - f(\tilde q)$, which are positive semidefinite kernels for every overlap structure.

steps.slogan: Interpolate from $M$ free spins to $M$ spins in cavity fields.
steps.detail: The interpolation $R_M(t)$ goes from $P_M$ to $G_M$, and integration by parts gives $R_M'(t) = \frac{\beta^2}{4}\mathbb{E}[f(q)-f(\tilde q)-(q-\tilde q)f'(\tilde q)] \ge 0$ by convexity.

steps.slogan: Control small Gaussian perturbations of a Hamiltonian by their variance.
steps.detail: Two uses of Jensen's inequality give $0 \le \mathbb{E}\log(Z(H+U)/Z(H)) \le \frac12\mathbb{E}U^2$ for an independent centered Gaussian perturbation $U$.

steps.slogan: Write the limit pressure as a limit of increments by superadditivity.
steps.detail: Superadditivity of $N P_N$ gives $\lim P_N = \lim_M\liminf_N M^{-1}\mathbb{E}\log(Z_{N+M}/Z_N)$, the free energy cost of adding $M$ spins.

steps.slogan: Show that a large system acts as a random overlap structure for $M$ added spins.
steps.detail: Splitting $K_{N+M}$ into reservoir terms, cavity fields and a remainder of variance $O(M^2/N)$ shows that $M^{-1}\mathbb{E}\log(Z_{N+M}/Z_N)$ is $G_M$ of the reservoir up to $o(1)$.

statement: In Derrida's random energy model with $2^N$ [independent](c:iid-random-variables) energies of law $N(0, N/2)$, the free entropy $N^{-1}\log Z_N(\beta)$ converges [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence) to $\log 2 + \beta^2/4$ for $\beta \le 2\sqrt{\log 2}$ and to $\beta\sqrt{\log 2}$ above, a [phase transition](c:phase-transition) of the [free energy](c:free-energy).

hypotheses.text: For each $N$ the energies $E_\sigma$, $1 \le \sigma \le 2^N$, are independent with the [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) $N(0, N/2)$.
The [inverse temperature](c:inverse-temperature) $\beta \ge 0$ is fixed, and $Z_N(\beta) = \sum_\sigma e^{-\beta E_\sigma}$.

conclusion: Almost surely $\lim_{N\to\infty} N^{-1}\log Z_N(\beta) = \log 2 + \beta^2/4$ if $\beta \le \beta_c = 2\sqrt{\log 2}$, and $= \beta\sqrt{\log 2}$ if $\beta > \beta_c$.

proofs.name: First moment bounds and counting of energy levels
proofs.slogan: Bound $Z_N$ above by its mean and by the maximum, and below by the number of low energy levels.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every $\beta \ge 0$, with almost sure convergence for an arbitrary coupling of the different $N$.

roles.why: Independence makes the level count binomial, and the Gaussian tail $e^{-x^2/N}$ fixes the entropy $\log 2 - x^2$.
The value of $\beta$ decides whether the optimal energy level lies inside the populated range or at its edge.

steps.slogan: Bound $Z_N$ above by its mean with Markov's inequality and Borel-Cantelli.
steps.detail: Since $\mathbb{E} Z_N = 2^N e^{\beta^2 N/4}$, Markov's inequality gives $P(Z_N \ge e^{N(\log 2 + \beta^2/4 + \varepsilon)}) \le e^{-N\varepsilon}$, and the Borel-Cantelli lemma gives $\limsup N^{-1}\log Z_N \le \log 2 + \beta^2/4$.

steps.slogan: Show that the lowest energy per site is at least $-\sqrt{\log 2}$ asymptotically.
steps.detail: The Gaussian tail bound $P(X \ge x) \le e^{-x^2/N}$ and a union bound over $2^N$ levels make $P(M_N \ge N(\sqrt{\log 2}+\varepsilon))$ exponentially small, so $\limsup M_N/N \le \sqrt{\log 2}$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Compare $Z_N(\beta)$ with $Z_N(\beta_c)$ above the critical point to get the frozen upper bound.
steps.detail: For $\beta > \beta_c$ each term satisfies $e^{\beta X_\sigma} \le e^{\beta_c X_\sigma}e^{(\beta-\beta_c)M_N}$, so $Z_N(\beta) \le e^{(\beta-\beta_c)M_N}Z_N(\beta_c)$, and the two previous bounds give $\beta\sqrt{\log 2}$.

steps.slogan: Count the levels below $-Nx$ with Chebyshev's inequality to bound $Z_N$ from below.
steps.detail: The count $K_N$ of levels below $-Nx$ is binomial with mean about $e^{N(\log 2 - x^2)}$, so Chebyshev and Borel-Cantelli give $K_N > \mathbb{E}K_N/2$ eventually, and $Z_N \ge K_N e^{\beta N x}$ gives the rate $\log 2 - x^2 + \beta x$.

steps.slogan: Optimize the counting bound over the energy level $x$ and match the upper bounds.
steps.detail: The maximum of $\log 2 - x^2 + \beta x$ over $0 \le x < \sqrt{\log 2}$ is $\log 2 + \beta^2/4$ for $\beta < \beta_c$ and tends to $\beta\sqrt{\log 2}$ otherwise, which matches the upper bounds in both phases.

statement: For a [Wigner matrix](c:wigner-matrix) whose entries have all moments finite, the [empirical measure](c:empirical-measure) of the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) converges [weakly](c:weak-convergence), [in probability](c:convergence-in-probability), to the [semicircle distribution](c:semicircle-distribution) with density $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^2}$ on $[-2,2]$.

hypotheses.text: The entries above the diagonal are [iid](c:iid-random-variables) variables $Z_{ij}/\sqrt N$ with mean $0$ and $\mathbb{E} Z_{12}^2 = 1$. The diagonal entries are iid variables $Y_i/\sqrt N$ with mean $0$, independent of the $Z_{ij}$.
Every absolute [moment](c:moment) $\mathbb{E}|Z_{12}|^k$ and $\mathbb{E}|Y_1|^k$ is finite.
The matrix $X_N$ is [symmetric](c:symmetric-matrix), so its eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N$ are real.

conclusion: For every bounded continuous $f$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, $P\left(\left|\frac1N\sum_i f(\lambda_i) - \int f\,d\sigma\right| > \varepsilon\right) \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$.

proofs.name: Moment method with closed walks, trees and Dyck paths
proofs.slogan: Write each moment of the spectrum as a sum over closed walks, keep the tree walks, count them by Catalan numbers, then approximate by polynomials.
proofs.scope: The full statement when all moments of the entries are finite.

roles.why: Independence and mean zero kill every walk that uses an edge once, and unit variance makes each tree walk count $1$.
Finite moments bound every term by a constant times a power of $N$, so the power counting works.
Symmetry gives real eigenvalues and the identity $\int x^k\,dL_N = N^{-1}\operatorname{tr} X_N^k$.

steps.slogan: Write each moment of $L_N$ as a sum over closed walks of length $k$.
steps.detail: The identity $\int x^k\,dL_N = N^{-1}\sum_{i_1,\dots,i_k} X_N(i_1,i_2)\cdots X_N(i_k,i_1)$ turns the moment into a sum over closed walks, and a walk that uses some edge once has expectation $0$.

steps.slogan: Show by power counting that only walks on trees with doubled edges survive.
steps.detail: A class of walks with $t$ distinct vertices contributes $O(N^{t-1-k/2})$, and $t \le k/2+1$, so only $k = 2m$ and walks on trees with $m$ edges, each crossed twice, remain in the limit.

steps.slogan: Code these tree walks by Dyck paths and count them by Catalan numbers.
steps.detail: The distance to the start of the walk is a Dyck path that determines the walk, and the reflection principle gives $C_m = \frac{(2m)!}{m!(m+1)!}$ such paths of length $2m$.

steps.slogan: Show that the moments of the semicircle are the Catalan numbers.
steps.detail: With $x = 2\sin\theta$ and integration by parts, the even moments satisfy $\mu_{2m}/\mu_{2m-2} = 4(2m-1)/(2m+2)$, the same recursion as the Catalan numbers.

steps.slogan: Show that each random moment concentrates around its mean with variance of order $1/N$.
steps.detail: Two walks with nonzero covariance share an edge, so their union graph is connected with at most $k+1$ vertices, which gives a variance of order $N^{-1}$ and convergence in probability by Chebyshev's inequality.

steps.slogan: Pass from polynomials to bounded continuous functions with tails and Weierstrass approximation.
steps.detail: Catalan bounds $C_k \le 4^k$ make the mass of $L_N$ outside $[-5,5]$ negligible, and a polynomial close to $f$ on $[-5,5]$ transfers the moment limits to $f$.

new_concepts.name: empirical measure
new_concepts.reminder: The empirical measure of a sample puts mass $1/n$ at each of the $n$ sample points.
new_concepts.definition: For random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with values in a measurable space $S$, the empirical measure is the random [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$, where $\delta_x$ is the [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) at $x$. So $\mu_n(A)$ is the fraction of the sample points that lie in $A$. If the $X_i$ are [iid](c:iid-random-variables) with law $\mu$ on a Polish space, then $\mu_n\to\mu$ weakly almost surely.

new_concepts.name: semicircle distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The semicircle distribution has density $\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^2}$ on $[-2,2]$, and its even moments are the Catalan numbers.
new_concepts.definition: The standard semicircle distribution is the probability distribution on $\mathbb R$ with [density](c:probability-density-function) $\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^2}$ on $[-2,2]$ and $0$ outside. Its odd [moments](c:moment) are $0$, and its moment of order $2k$ is the [Catalan number](c:catalan-number) $C_k=\frac1{k+1}\binom{2k}k$. It is the limit of the empirical spectral measures of normalized [Wigner matrices](c:wigner-matrix), and it is the central limit law of free probability.

new_concepts.name: Wigner matrix
new_concepts.reminder: A Wigner matrix is a symmetric random matrix with independent centered entries on and above the diagonal.
new_concepts.definition: A real Wigner matrix of size $N$ is a [symmetric](c:symmetric-matrix) [random matrix](c:random-matrix) $X=(X_{ij})$ such that the entries $X_{ij}$ with $i\le j$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables), the entries above the diagonal are centered with variance $1$, and the diagonal entries are centered with finite variance. Often the entries above the diagonal are identically distributed, and the complex Hermitian version is defined in the same way. Wigner's theorem states that the empirical spectral measure of $X/\sqrt N$ converges to the [semicircle distribution](c:semicircle-distribution).

statement: For the eigenvalues of a $\beta$-ensemble with a confining potential $V$, the [empirical measure](c:empirical-measure) satisfies a [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology) with speed $N^2$ and good [rate function](c:rate-function) $I(\mu) = \int V\,d\mu - \frac{\beta}{2}\iint \log|x-y|\,\mu(dx)\mu(dy) - c$.

hypotheses.text: The exponent $\beta > 0$ is fixed, and the points have the joint density proportional to $\prod_{i<j}|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|^\beta e^{-N\sum_i V(\lambda_i)}$, like the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of the GOE or the GUE.
The potential $V$ is continuous and $\liminf_{|x|\to\infty} V(x)/(\beta'\log|x|) > 1$ for some $\beta' > 1$ with $\beta' \ge \beta$.

conclusion: For every open set $O$ and closed set $F$ of [probability measures](c:probability-measure), $\liminf N^{-2}\log P(L_N \in O) \ge -\inf_O I$ and $\limsup N^{-2}\log P(L_N \in F) \le -\inf_F I$, and $I$ has compact level sets.

proofs.name: Coulomb gas energy with truncation, localization and exponential tightness
proofs.slogan: Write the density as $e^{-N^2 \cdot \text{energy}}$, truncate the log singularity for the upper bound, and freeze the points at quantiles for the lower bound.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 2.6.1 in Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni (2010), Section 2.6.1, after Ben Arous and Guionnet (1997). Lemma 2.6.2 and Appendix D of the source are cited.

roles.why: The Vandermonde factor $|\Delta|^\beta$ turns the density into $e^{-N^2}$ times a pair energy of the empirical measure.
The growth of $V$ beats the logarithm, so the pair energy is bounded below and confines the points.

steps.slogan: Write the joint density as $e^{-N^2}$ times a pair energy of $L_N$.
steps.detail: With $f(x,y) = \frac12 V(x) + \frac12 V(y) - \frac{\beta}{2}\log|x-y|$, the density is $(Z^N)^{-1}\exp(-N^2\iint_{x\ne y} f\,dL_N\,dL_N)\prod_i e^{-V(\lambda_i)}$, so only the singularities of $f$ stop a direct use of Varadhan's lemma.

steps.slogan: Show that $I$ is a good, strictly convex rate function with one minimizer.
steps.detail: Lemma 2.6.2 of the source shows that $f$ is bounded below, that $I = \sup_M \iint (f\wedge M) - c$ is [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuous-function), that its level sets are tight, and that $I$ is strictly [convex](c:convex-function).

steps.slogan: Prove exponential tightness at speed $N^2$ with a bound on $\int|V|\,dL_N$.
steps.detail: Jensen's inequality gives $\log Z^N \ge -CN^2$, and $f(x,y) \ge a|V(x)| + a|V(y)| + c'$ makes $P(\int|V|\,dL_N \ge M)$ at most $e^{-(2aM - C')N^2}$ times $e^{O(N)}$.

steps.slogan: Bound small balls from above with the truncated energy $f \wedge M$.
steps.detail:
The diagonal adds only $M/N$ to the truncated energy, the functional $
u \mapsto \iint (f\wedge M)\,d
u\,d
u$ is continuous, and monotone convergence in $M$ gives the bound $-\iint f\,d\mu\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Bound small balls from below by freezing each point near a quantile of $\mu$.
steps.detail: For compactly supported $\mu$ without atoms, the points stay within $\delta/2$ of the quantiles $x_{i,N}$, the volume cost is only $e^{O(N\log N)}$, and Riemann sums give the bound $-\iint f\,d\mu\,d\mu$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\lim N^{-2}\log Z^N = -c$ and upgrade the weak principle with tightness.
steps.detail: The two ball bounds give $\lim N^{-2}\log Z^N = -c$ and the weak principle with rate $I$, and exponential tightness turns the weak [large deviation principle](c:large-deviation-principle) into the full principle.

concepts.c:empirical-measure: The random empirical measure of the points is the object whose deviations are measured.
concepts.c:large-deviation-principle: The theorem is a large deviation principle at speed N squared.
concepts.c:weak-topology: Open and closed sets of measures are taken in the weak topology.
concepts.c:rate-function: The logarithmic energy minus its minimum is the rate function.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: For the Gaussian ensembles the points are the eigenvalues of a random matrix.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The principle lives on the space of probability measures on the real line.
concepts.c:lower-semicontinuous-function: Lower semicontinuity of the rate function makes the closed set bound possible.
concepts.c:convex-function: Strict convexity of the rate function gives a unique equilibrium measure.

new_concepts.name: empirical measure
new_concepts.reminder: The empirical measure of a sample puts mass $1/n$ at each of the $n$ sample points.
new_concepts.definition: For random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with values in a measurable space $S$, the empirical measure is the random [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$, where $\delta_x$ is the [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) at $x$. So $\mu_n(A)$ is the fraction of the sample points that lie in $A$. If the $X_i$ are [iid](c:iid-random-variables) with law $\mu$ on a Polish space, then $\mu_n\to\mu$ weakly almost surely.

statement: For independent [exponential](c:exponential-distribution) weights with mean $1$ and $\gamma \ge 1$, the last-passage time $H([\gamma N], N)$, centred at $(1+\sqrt{\gamma})^2 N$ and divided by $\gamma^{-1/6}(1+\sqrt{\gamma})^{4/3} N^{1/3}$, converges in law to the [Tracy-Widom distribution](c:tracy-widom-distribution).

hypotheses.text: The weights $u(i,j)$ are independent [exponential](c:exponential-distribution) random variables with mean $1$.
The sides of the rectangle are $M = [\gamma N]$ and $N$, with a constant $\gamma \ge 1$.

conclusion: $P\Big[\dfrac{H([\gamma N], N) - (1+\sqrt{\gamma})^2 N}{\gamma^{-1/6}(1+\sqrt{\gamma})^{4/3} N^{1/3}} \le s\Big] \to F(s) = \det(I - A)_{L^2[s,\infty)}$ for every $s \in \mathbb{R}$, where $A$ is the Airy kernel.

proofs.name: RSK, Laguerre ensemble and Airy kernel asymptotics
proofs.slogan: RSK identifies last-passage times with largest eigenvalues of a Laguerre ensemble, whose kernel converges to the Airy kernel at the edge.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof of (1.22) in Johansson (2000). The kernel limit and the Fredholm series estimates are cited from the source.

roles.why: Exponential weights are limits of geometric weights, for which the matrix is uniform given its sum and RSK gives an exact formula.
The ratio $\gamma$ fixes the Laguerre parameter $\alpha_N = [\gamma N] - N$, the edge $(1+\sqrt{\gamma})^2 N$ and the scale.

steps.slogan: The Knuth correspondence turns geometric last-passage times into first rows of [Young tableau](c:young-tableau) shapes.
steps.detail: Given its entry sum, the geometric weight matrix is uniform, and RSK maps it to tableau pairs with $G(M,N) = \lambda_1$. Counting semistandard tableaux gives the Meixner ensemble formula of Proposition 1.3.

steps.slogan: A geometric-to-exponential limit gives the largest eigenvalue law of a Laguerre [random matrix](c:random-matrix) ensemble.
steps.detail: With $q = 1 - 1/L$ and $L \to \infty$, the Meixner sum becomes $P[H(M,N) \le t] = Z^{-1}\int_{[0,t]^N} \prod_{i<j}(x_i - x_j)^2 \prod_j x_j^{M-N} e^{-x_j}\,d^N x$.

steps.slogan: Orthogonal polynomials write this probability as a [Fredholm determinant](c:fredholm-determinant) of the Laguerre kernel.
steps.detail: The Christoffel-Darboux kernel $K_N^{\alpha_N}$ of the weight $x^{\alpha_N} e^{-x}$ gives the Fredholm series (1.23) for $P[H \le cN + \rho N^{1/3} s]$ with $c = (1+\sqrt{\gamma})^2$.

steps.slogan: At the spectral edge the rescaled Laguerre kernel converges to the [Airy](c:airy-function) kernel.
steps.detail: A saddle point analysis of the contour integral for $L_n^{\alpha}$ near $x = cN$ gives (1.24). The source states this limit and refers to its Meixner analysis for the method.

steps.slogan: Trace bounds and kernel convergence pass the Fredholm series to the limit $\det(I - A)$.
steps.detail: Lemma 3.1 of the source uses positive definiteness, $|\det K| \le \prod K(x_j,x_j)$, and trace bounds to truncate the series. Uniform kernel convergence on compact sets then gives the limit $F(s)$.

new_concepts.name: exponential distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ on $[0,\infty)$ and no memory.
new_concepts.definition: For $\lambda>0$, the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ is the law on $[0,\infty)$ with [probability density function](c:probability-density-function) $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, so $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ and $E[X]=1/\lambda$. Among laws of positive random variables, it is the only one with the memoryless property $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$ for all $s,t\ge0$.

new_concepts.name: Tracy–Widom distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The limit law of the centred and rescaled largest eigenvalue of a large Gaussian unitary random matrix.
new_concepts.definition: The Tracy-Widom distribution ($\beta = 2$) is the law on $\mathbb{R}$ with distribution function $F_2(s) = \det(I - A)_{L^2[s,\infty)} = \exp\big(-\int_s^\infty (x - s)\, u(x)^2\, dx\big)$. Here $A$ is the Airy kernel $A(x,y) = (\operatorname{Ai}(x)\operatorname{Ai}'(y) - \operatorname{Ai}'(x)\operatorname{Ai}(y))/(x - y)$, and $u$ is the Hastings-McLeod solution of the [Painlevé](c:painleve-transcendent) II equation $u'' = 2u^3 + xu$ with $u(x)^2 \sim \operatorname{Ai}(x)^2$ as $x \to +\infty$.

statement: For a uniformly random [permutation](c:permutation) of $N$ letters with longest increasing subsequence $l_N$, the law of $(l_N - 2\sqrt{N})/N^{1/6}$ converges to the [Tracy-Widom distribution](c:tracy-widom-distribution) $F$ of the largest GUE eigenvalue.

hypotheses.text: The permutation $\pi$ is uniformly distributed on the symmetric group $S_N$.

conclusion: $P\big((l_N - 2\sqrt{N})/N^{1/6} \le t\big) \to F(t) = \exp\big(-\int_t^\infty (x - t) u(x)^2\, dx\big)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, where $u'' = 2u^3 + xu$ and $u(x) \sim -\operatorname{Ai}(x)$ as $x \to +\infty$.

proofs.name: Toeplitz determinant and Riemann-Hilbert steepest descent
proofs.slogan: Gessel's identity turns the Poissonized law into a Toeplitz determinant, and steepest descent on its Riemann-Hilbert problem produces Painlevé II.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in Baik, Deift and Johansson (1999). The steepest descent estimates (Lemmas 5.1, 6.3 and 7.1) and the de-Poissonization lemmas are cited.

roles.why: Under the uniform law the Schensted correspondence gives $P(l_N \le n)$ as a sum of squared tableau counts, which leads to Gessel's identity.

steps.slogan: Poissonize $N$ and write $P(L(\lambda) \le n)$ as a [Toeplitz determinant](c:toeplitz-determinant).
steps.detail: The Schensted correspondence gives $P(l_N \le n) = \frac{1}{N!}\sum f(\mu)^2$ over [Young tableau](c:young-tableau) shapes with first row at most $n$. Appendix A of the source then proves $\varphi_n(\lambda) = e^{-\lambda} D_{n-1}(\lambda)$ for the weight $e^{2\sqrt{\lambda}\cos\theta}$.

steps.slogan: Szegő's strong limit theorem writes $\log \varphi_n$ as a sum of orthogonal polynomial coefficients.
steps.detail: The leading coefficients satisfy $\kappa_k^2 = D_{k-1}/D_k$ and $D_k(\lambda) \to e^\lambda$ as $k \to \infty$. The product telescopes to $\log \varphi_n(\lambda) = \sum_{k \ge n} \log \kappa_k^2(\lambda)$.

steps.slogan: A $2 \times 2$ [Riemann-Hilbert problem](c:riemann-hilbert-problem) on the unit circle encodes each coefficient $\kappa_k^2$.
steps.detail: One has $\kappa_k^2 = -Y_{21}(0; k+1, \lambda)$. The equilibrium measure for $\gamma = 2\sqrt{\lambda}/(k+1)$ fills the circle when $\gamma \le 1$ and an arc when $\gamma > 1$, and its $g$-function normalizes the problem.

steps.slogan: Steepest descent gives $\kappa_k^2$, with a [Painlevé II](c:painleve-transcendent) parametrix at $\gamma = 1$.
steps.detail: Lemmas 5.1 and 6.3 of the source show that $\kappa_{q-1}^2$ is exponentially close to $1$ away from $\gamma = 1$, and equals $1 + i2^{4/3}q^{-1/3} m^{PII}_{1,22}(t) + O(q^{-2/3})$ in the critical window.

steps.slogan: Summing over $k \ge n$ turns the window estimates into an integral of the Painlevé function.
steps.detail: Lemma 7.1 of the source gives $\log \varphi_n(\lambda) \to \int_t^\infty 2i\, m^{PII}_{1,22}(y)\,dy$ when $t = 2^{1/3}(n+1)^{2/3}(1 - 2\sqrt{\lambda}/(n+1))$ stays bounded.

steps.slogan: Monotonicity in $N$ removes the Poissonization and identifies the limit as $F$.
steps.detail: Since $P(l_N \le n)$ decreases in $N$, Lemma 8.2 squeezes it between $\varphi_n$ at $N \pm O(\sqrt{N}\log N)$. Integration by parts with $(2i\,m^{PII}_{1,22})' = u^2$ gives the limit $F(t)$, built from the [Airy function](c:airy-function) asymptotics of $u$.

new_concepts.reminder: The limit law of the centred and rescaled largest eigenvalue of a large Gaussian unitary random matrix.
new_concepts.definition: The Tracy-Widom distribution ($\beta = 2$) is the law on $\mathbb{R}$ with distribution function $F_2(s) = \det(I - A)_{L^2[s,\infty)} = \exp\big(-\int_s^\infty (x - s)\, u(x)^2\, dx\big)$. Here $A$ is the Airy kernel $A(x,y) = (\operatorname{Ai}(x)\operatorname{Ai}'(y) - \operatorname{Ai}'(x)\operatorname{Ai}(y))/(x - y)$, and $u$ is the Hastings-McLeod solution of the [Painlevé](c:painleve-transcendent) II equation $u'' = 2u^3 + xu$ with $u(x)^2 \sim \operatorname{Ai}(x)^2$ as $x \to +\infty$.

statement: Let $X_n$ be a $p \times n$ [random matrix](c:random-matrix) with [iid](c:iid-random-variables) real entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, with $p/n \to y \in (0,\infty)$. Almost surely, the [empirical distribution](c:empirical-distribution) of the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of $S_n = \frac{1}{n} X_n X_n^{\top}$ [converges weakly](c:weak-convergence-of-measures) to the Marchenko-Pastur law $\mu_y$.

hypotheses.text: The entries of $X_n$ are [independent copies](c:iid-random-variables) of a real variable $\xi$ with $\mathbb{E}\xi = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}\xi^2 = 1$.
The dimensions satisfy $p(n)/n \to y$ for a constant $y \in (0, \infty)$.

conclusion: Almost surely $\mu_n \to \mu_y$ weakly, where $\mu_y = (1 - 1/y)^+ \delta_0 + \frac{\sqrt{(x-a)(b-x)}}{2\pi y x} \mathbf{1}_{[a,b]}(x)\,dx$ with $a = (1-\sqrt{y})^2$ and $b = (1+\sqrt{y})^2$.

proofs.name: Resolvent and Stieltjes transform method
proofs.slogan: Rank-one updates of the resolvent give a quadratic equation for the limit Stieltjes transform, and Stieltjes inversion reads off $\mu_y$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every $y \in (0, \infty)$ and every entry law with mean $0$ and variance $1$.

roles.why: Independent columns give the martingale differences, and independent entries with variance one make $x^\top B x$ close to $\operatorname{tr} B$.
The ratio $p/n \to y$ fixes the coefficients of the limit equation and makes the deviation bounds summable.

steps.slogan: Bound the [resolvent](c:resolvent) of a [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix) matrix and its rank-one updates.
steps.detail: Diagonalize $C$. Then $\|(C - z)^{-1}\| \le 1/v$, $\operatorname{Im}(z(1 + w^\top (C - z)^{-1} w)) \ge v$, and by Sherman-Morrison a rank-one update changes $\operatorname{tr}(C - z)^{-1}$ by at most $1/v$.

steps.slogan: A quadratic form $x^\top B x$ in independent entries stays close to $\operatorname{tr} B$.
steps.detail: The off-diagonal part has second moment at most $2p\|B\|^2$. Truncation of $X_k^2 - 1$ at level $p^{1/4}$ controls the diagonal part, so $\mathbb{E}|x^\top B x - \operatorname{tr} B| \le \|B\| p \varepsilon_p$ with $\varepsilon_p \to 0$.

steps.slogan: A [martingale](c:martingale) over the columns concentrates $s_n(z)$ around its mean.
steps.detail: Revealing one column at a time gives martingale differences bounded by $2/(pv)$. Azuma-Hoeffding and Borel-Cantelli give $s_n(z) - \mathbb{E}s_n(z) \to 0$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: The identity $G(S_n - z) = I$ and Sherman-Morrison give an approximate equation for $\mathbb{E}s_n$.
steps.detail: One gets $y_n(1 + z s_n) = 1 - \frac{1}{n}\sum_k (1 + q_k)^{-1}$ with $q_k = \frac1n x_k^\top G_k x_k$. Each $q_k$ is close to $y_n \mathbb{E}s_n$, so $y_n(1 + z t_n) - 1 + (1 + y_n t_n)^{-1} \to 0$.

steps.slogan: The sign of $\operatorname{Im}(zt)$ selects one root of the limit quadratic equation.
steps.detail: Limits satisfy $yzt^2 + (y + z - 1)t + 1 = 0$ with roots $(1 - y - z \pm R(z))/(2yz)$. Since $\operatorname{Im} R(z) \ge v$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z t) \ge 0$, only the root $r(z)$ with $+R$ remains.

steps.slogan: The bound $|z r(z) + 1| \le 1/v$ gives [tightness](c:tightness) and limit points with transform $r$.
steps.detail: Since $\mu(|\lambda| \ge w) \le 2(1 - w \operatorname{Im}s_\mu(iw))$, the sequence $\mu_n$ is tight on an almost sure event. Prokhorov gives weak limit points $\nu$, and $s_\nu = r$ on the upper half-plane.

steps.slogan: Stieltjes inversion of $r$ shows that every limit point equals the Marchenko-Pastur law.
steps.detail: Boundary values of $\operatorname{Im} r(x + iv)/\pi$ give the density $\sqrt{(x-a)(b-x)}/(2\pi y x)$ on $(a, b)$, and the pole $-A/z$ gives the atom $A = (1 - 1/y)^+$ at $0$. So every limit point is $\mu_y$.

statement: For a [Galton-Watson branching process](c:branching-process) with offspring [generating function](c:generating-function) $f$, mean $m$ and $p_1 \ne 1$, the extinction probability $q$ is the smallest [fixed point](c:fixed-point) of $f$ in $[0,1]$, and $q = 1$ if and only if $m \le 1$.

hypotheses.text: The process starts from $Z_0 = 1$, and all individuals have [independent](c:independent-random-variables) numbers of children with the common law $(p_k)_{k \ge 0}$.
The offspring law is not the point mass at one: $p_1 \ne 1$.

conclusion: $q = \min\{s \in [0,1] : f(s) = s\}$. Also $q = 1$ if and only if $m \le 1$, and for $m > 1$ the number $q < 1$ is the only root of $f(s) = s$ in $[0,1)$.

proofs.name: Iteration of the generating function
proofs.slogan: The extinction probabilities by generation $n$ iterate $f$ from $0$, so they climb to the smallest fixed point of $f$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every offspring law with $p_1 \ne 1$, including infinite mean.

roles.why: Independence of the offspring numbers makes the generating function of $Z_n$ the $n$-fold composition of $f$.
With $m = 1$ and $p_1 \ne 1$ some $p_k$ with $k \ge 2$ is positive, which gives $f(s) > s$ below $1$.

steps.slogan: The [generating function](c:generating-function) of $Z_n$ is the $n$-fold composition of $f$.
steps.detail: Given $Z_{n-1} = j$, the next generation is a sum of $j$ independent offspring numbers, so $\mathbb{E}[s^{Z_n} \mid Z_{n-1}] = f(s)^{Z_{n-1}}$. Hence $q_n = P(Z_n = 0)$ satisfies $q_0 = 0$ and $q_{n+1} = f(q_n)$.

steps.slogan: The increasing limit $q$ of the iterates is the smallest [fixed point](c:fixed-point) of $f$.
steps.detail: The events $\{Z_n = 0\}$ increase to extinction, so $q = \lim q_n$ and continuity of $f$ gives $f(q) = q$. If $f(r) = r$, induction gives $q_n \le r$ because $f$ is nondecreasing, so $q \le r$.

steps.slogan: For mean at most one, the chord bound shows that $f$ has no fixed point below $1$.
steps.detail: The bound $1 - s^k \le k(1-s)$, strict for $k \ge 2$, gives $1 - f(s) \le m(1-s)$. If $m < 1$, or if $m = 1$ and some $p_k$ with $k \ge 2$ is positive, then $f(s) > s$ on $[0,1)$ and $q = 1$.

steps.slogan: For mean above one, $f$ dips below the diagonal near $1$ and has a root below $1$.
steps.detail: The difference quotient $(1 - f(s))/(1-s)$ increases to $m > 1$ by monotone convergence, so $f(s_0) < s_0$ for some $s_0 < 1$. Since $f(0) \ge 0$, the intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point in $[0, s_0]$, so $q < 1$.

steps.slogan: Strict [convexity](c:convex-function) of $f$ leaves only one fixed point in $[0,1)$ when $m > 1$.
steps.detail: For $m > 1$ some $p_k$ with $k \ge 2$ is positive, so $f(s) - s$ is strictly convex and has at most two roots in $[0,1]$, one of them at $1$. With the previous steps, $q$ is the smallest root, it equals $1$ exactly when $m \le 1$, and it is the unique root in $[0,1)$ otherwise.

concepts.c:branching-process: The Galton-Watson process is the population model whose extinction the theorem decides.
concepts.c:generating-function: The offspring generating function turns the generation recursion into iteration of one function.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The extinction probability is identified as the smallest fixed point of $f$.

new_concepts.name: Galton-Watson branching process
new_concepts.reminder: In a Galton–Watson process each individual has an independent random number of children with one fixed offspring law.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(\xi_{n,i})_{n,i\ge1}$ be [iid](c:iid-random-variables) random variables with values in $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ and offspring law $p_k=\mathbb P(\xi=k)$. The Galton–Watson process is $Z_0=1$ and $Z_{n+1}=\sum_{i=1}^{Z_n}\xi_{n+1,i}$, the size of generation $n+1$. If $p_1\ne1$, the extinction probability is the smallest root in $[0,1]$ of $f(s)=s$, where $f(s)=\sum_kp_ks^k$ is the [generating function](c:generating-function), and it equals $1$ exactly when the mean $m=\mathbb E\xi$ satisfies $m\le1$.

statement: For a supercritical [Galton-Watson branching process](c:branching-process) with offspring variable $L$ and mean $1 < m < \infty$, the [martingale](c:martingale) $Z_n/m^n$ has an [almost sure](c:almost-sure-convergence) limit $W$. The conditions $P(W=0) = q$, $\mathbb{E}W = 1$ and $\mathbb{E}[L \log^+ L] < \infty$ are equivalent, and $W = 0$ almost surely when $\mathbb{E}[L \log^+ L] = \infty$.

hypotheses.text: The process starts from $Z_0 = 1$, and all individuals have [independent](c:independent-random-variables) numbers of children with the common law $(p_k)_{k \ge 0}$ of $L$.
The mean number of children satisfies $1 < m = \mathbb{E}L < \infty$.

conclusion: $Z_n/m^n \to W$ almost surely, and $P(W = 0) = q \iff \mathbb{E}W = 1 \iff \mathbb{E}[L\log^+ L] < \infty$. If $\mathbb{E}[L\log^+ L] = \infty$, then $W = 0$ almost surely.

proofs.name: Size-biased Galton-Watson trees
proofs.slogan: Size-biasing turns the tree into a spine with immigration, and $\mathbb{E}W = 1$ exactly when this immigration grows slower than $m^n$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every offspring law with $1 < m < \infty$.

roles.why: Independent offspring numbers make $Z_n/m^n$ a martingale and make the bushes off the spine independent Galton-Watson trees.
A finite mean defines the size-biased law $k p_k/m$, and $m > 1$ gives the geometric scale and the root $q < 1$.

steps.slogan: The normalized population $W_n = Z_n/m^n$ is a nonnegative [martingale](c:martingale) and converges almost surely.
steps.detail: Each of the $Z_n$ individuals has mean $m$ children, so $\mathbb{E}[Z_{n+1} \mid Z_n] = m Z_n$. Doob's theorem gives $W_n \to W < \infty$ almost surely, and Fatou gives $\mathbb{E}W \le 1$.

steps.slogan: The size-biased [tree](c:rooted-tree) law has [density](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) $W_n$ with respect to the Galton-Watson law on $n$ levels.
steps.detail: Give the spine vertex $\hat L$ children with $P(\hat L = k) = k p_k/m$, choose the next spine vertex uniformly, and attach Galton-Watson trees elsewhere. Induction on $n$ shows $\widehat{GW}[t]_n = W_n(t)\, GW[t]_n$.

steps.slogan: The size-biased behaviour of $W$ decides between $\mathbb{E}W = 1$ and $W = 0$.
steps.detail: If $W < \infty$ under $\widehat{GW}$, then $\sup_n \widehat{GW}(W_n > K) \to 0$, so $(W_n)$ is uniformly integrable under $GW$ and Vitali gives $\mathbb{E}W = 1$. If $W = \infty$ under $\widehat{GW}$, Fatou on $\{\sup_j W_j \le K\}$ gives $W = 0$ under $GW$.

steps.slogan: Off the spine, the size-biased tree is a branching process with immigration $Y_k = \hat L_k - 1$.
steps.detail: The siblings of the spine vertices start independent Galton-Watson trees. With the immigration fixed by Fubini, $(Z_n - 1)/m^n$ is a submartingale with mean $\sum_{k \le n} Y_k m^{-k}$, so it converges when this series converges.

steps.slogan: Borel-Cantelli compares the immigration $Y_k$ with $m^k$ through the moment $\mathbb{E}[L\log^+ L]$.
steps.detail: Here $\mathbb{E}\log^+ Y_1 = m^{-1}\mathbb{E}[L \log^+(L-1)]$, which is finite exactly when $\mathbb{E}[L\log^+L] < \infty$. Then $Y_k \le m^{k/2}$ eventually and $W < \infty$. Otherwise $Y_k > K m^k$ infinitely often and $W = \infty$, both under $\widehat{GW}$.

steps.slogan: The probability $P(W = 0)$ is a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) of $f$, hence equal to $q$ or $1$.
steps.detail: The limit satisfies $W = m^{-1}\sum_{i \le Z_1} W^{(i)}$ with independent copies $W^{(i)}$, so $P(W=0) = f(P(W=0))$. With the two previous steps this closes the cycle of equivalences, because $q < 1$ when $m > 1$.

concepts.c:martingale: The normalized population $Z_n/m^n$ is a martingale, which gives the limit $W$.

concepts.c:rooted-tree: The proof works on the space of rooted family trees, not only with generation sizes.

statement: [Simple random walk](c:random-walk) on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is [recurrent](c:recurrence) for $d = 1, 2$ and transient for $d \ge 3$. The expected number of visits to the origin is $(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^d} \frac{dt}{1 - \varphi(t)}$ with $\varphi(t) = \frac{1}{d}\sum_j \cos t_j$.

hypotheses.text: The walk starts at the origin, $S_0 = 0$.
The steps $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and uniform on the $2d$ vectors $\pm e_1, \dots, \pm e_d$.

conclusion: $\sum_{n \ge 0} P(S_n = 0) = \frac{1}{1-\rho} = (2\pi)^{-d}\int_{[-\pi,\pi]^d} \frac{dt}{1-\varphi(t)}$, which is infinite exactly when $d \le 2$. So $\rho = 1$ for $d \le 2$ and $\rho < 1$ for $d \ge 3$.

proofs.name: Fourier integral for the Green function
proofs.slogan: Count visits to the origin, write their mean as a Fourier integral, and test whether $1/|t|^2$ is integrable near zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem in every dimension $d \ge 1$, with the formula for the expected number of visits.

roles.why: Returns are counted at the starting point, and the walk restarted at each return has the same law.
Independent uniform steps give the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) $\varphi(t)^n$ of $S_n$ and the bounds on $1 - \varphi$.

steps.slogan: The number of returns to the origin is geometric with ratio $\rho$.
steps.detail: The walk after the $k$-th return is a fresh copy of the walk, so $P(\tau_k < \infty) = \rho^k$. Tonelli's theorem gives $G = \sum_n P(S_n = 0) = \sum_k \rho^k = 1/(1-\rho)$, so the walk is [recurrent](c:recurrence) exactly when $G = \infty$.

steps.slogan: Write each return probability as an integral of a power of the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function).
steps.detail: Independence gives $\mathbb{E} e^{i t\cdot S_n} = \varphi(t)^n$, and orthogonality of the [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) characters on the torus gives $P(S_n = 0) = (2\pi)^{-d}\int \varphi(t)^n\,dt$.

steps.slogan: Sum the return probabilities with a damping factor $r$ and let $r$ increase to one.
steps.detail: For $r < 1$ the geometric series gives $\sum_n r^n P(S_n = 0) = (2\pi)^{-d}\int dt/(1 - r\varphi)$. Monotone convergence on $\{\varphi \ge 0\}$ and dominated convergence on $\{\varphi < 0\}$ give $G = (2\pi)^{-d}\int dt/(1-\varphi)$.

steps.slogan: Compare $1 - \varphi(t)$ with $|t|^2$ on the whole torus by Jordan's inequality.
steps.detail: From $1 - \cos u = 2\sin^2(u/2)$ and Jordan's inequality, $2u^2/\pi^2 \le 1 - \cos u \le u^2/2$ for $|u| \le \pi$. Averaging gives $2|t|^2/(\pi^2 d) \le 1 - \varphi(t) \le |t|^2/(2d)$.

steps.slogan: The integral of $|t|^{-2}$ near the origin diverges exactly in dimensions one and two.
steps.detail: In polar coordinates $\int_{|t| \le R} |t|^{-2}\,dt$ is a multiple of $\int_0^R r^{d-3}\,dr$, which is infinite for $d \le 2$ and finite for $d \ge 3$. So $G = \infty$ and $\rho = 1$ for $d \le 2$, while $G < \infty$ and $\rho = 1 - 1/G < 1$ for $d \ge 3$.

concepts.c:recurrence: Recurrence means return to the start with probability one, the property that the theorem decides.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independent steps make the characteristic function of $S_n$ a power of $\varphi$.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: The characteristic function $\varphi$ of one step turns the Green function into an integral.
concepts.c:fourier-series: Orthogonality of the characters $e^{i t\cdot x}$ on the torus extracts the probability of the origin.

new_concepts.name: recurrent Markov chain
new_concepts.reminder: A Markov chain is recurrent when it returns to its starting state with probability one.
new_concepts.definition: A state $x$ of a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) is recurrent if $\mathbb P_x(\tau_x^+<\infty)=1$, where $\tau_x^+=\min\{n\ge1:X_n=x\}$ is the return time, and it is transient otherwise. Equivalently, $x$ is recurrent exactly when $\sum_{n\ge0}P^n(x,x)=\infty$, that is, when the expected number of visits to $x$ is infinite. In an irreducible chain all states are recurrent or all are transient, and the chain is called recurrent or transient accordingly.

statement: In a locally finite [electrical network](c:electrical-network), if disjoint edge cutsets $\Pi_k$ separate $a$ from infinity, then the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) from $a$ to infinity is at least $\sum_k \bigl(\sum_{e \in \Pi_k} c(e)\bigr)^{-1}$. If this sum is infinite, the network is [recurrent](c:recurrence).

hypotheses.text: The [graph](c:graph) $G$ is infinite, connected and locally finite, with conductances $c(e) \in (0, \infty)$.
The edge sets $\Pi_1, \Pi_2, \dots$ are pairwise disjoint, and each meets every infinite simple path from $a$.

conclusion: $R(a \leftrightarrow \infty) = \bigl(\pi(a) P_a(\tau_a^+ = \infty)\bigr)^{-1} \ge \sum_k s_k^{-1}$ with $s_k = \sum_{e \in \Pi_k} c(e)$. If $\sum_k s_k^{-1} = \infty$, the walk returns to $a$ almost surely.

proofs.name: Energy of the unit current on disjoint cutsets
proofs.slogan: A unit current must cross each cutset, and Cauchy-Schwarz makes each crossing cost energy at least the inverse conductance of the cutset.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for finite or infinite cutsets in a locally finite network.

roles.why: Local finiteness makes the balls finite and lets Kőnig's lemma turn separation from infinity into separation from a far sphere.
Each cutset carries the whole unit current, and disjointness lets the energies on the cutsets add up.

steps.slogan: Build the voltage and the current from $a$ to the sphere of radius $m$.
steps.detail: The voltage $v(x) = P_x(\tau_a < \tau_{Z_m})$ is a [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) off $\{a\} \cup Z_m$ by the Markov property. The current $i(x,y) = c(x,y)(v(x) - v(y))$ has divergence $0$ off the ends and $I_m = \pi(a)(1 - P_a(\tau_a^+ < \tau_{Z_m}))$ at $a$.

steps.slogan: The unit current flow from $a$ to the sphere has energy $1/I_m$.
steps.detail: Summation by parts gives $\sum_e c(e)(v(x)-v(y))^2 = \sum_x v(x)\,\mathrm{div}\, i(x) = I_m$. So the [flow](c:flow) $\theta = i/I_m$ has unit strength and energy $\sum_e r(e)\theta(e)^2 = 1/I_m$.

steps.slogan: Each separating cutset carries the unit flow and therefore costs energy.
steps.detail: Summing the divergence of $\theta$ over the vertices that $a$ reaches without the cutset gives $\sum_{e \in \Pi}|\theta(e)| \ge 1$. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality then gives $\sum_{e\in\Pi} r(e)\theta(e)^2 \ge (\sum_{e\in\Pi} c(e))^{-1}$, and disjoint cutsets add.

steps.slogan: Kőnig's lemma makes each cutset separate $a$ from all far spheres.
steps.detail: The component of $a$ after removal of $\Pi_k$ cannot be infinite, since Kőnig's lemma would give an infinite simple path that avoids $\Pi_k$. So for $m$ large every path from $a$ to $Z_m$ crosses each of $\Pi_1, \dots, \Pi_N$.

steps.slogan: Bound the escape probability by $I_m$ and let the number of cutsets grow.
steps.detail: Escape to infinity forces $\tau_a^+ \ge \tau_{Z_m}$, so $\pi(a)P_a(\tau_a^+ = \infty) \le I_m \le (\sum_{k \le N} s_k^{-1})^{-1}$ for large $m$. Letting $N \to \infty$ gives the bound on the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) and recurrence when the series diverges.

concepts.c:effective-resistance: The effective resistance to infinity is the inverse of the escape rate that the theorem bounds.
concepts.c:recurrence: Recurrence of the walk is the conclusion when the series of inverse cutset conductances diverges.
concepts.c:graph: Cutsets and paths are defined in the underlying locally finite graph.
concepts.c:harmonic-function: The voltage is harmonic off the source and the sink, which makes the current divergence free.
concepts.c:flow: The normalized current is a unit flow whose energy equals the effective resistance.

new_concepts.name: effective resistance
new_concepts.reminder: The effective resistance between two vertices is the voltage drop per unit current that flows between them.
new_concepts.definition: In a finite [electrical network](c:electrical-network), let $v$ be the voltage that is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) off $\{a,z\}$ with $v(a)=1$ and $v(z)=0$, and let $\|i\|$ be the strength of the resulting current from $a$ to $z$. The effective resistance is $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(a\leftrightarrow z)=1/\|i\|=1/(c(a)\,\mathbb P_a(\tau_z<\tau_a^+))$. By Thomson's principle, it is also the minimum of the energy $\sum_er(e)\theta(e)^2$ over unit flows $\theta$ from $a$ to $z$.

new_concepts.name: electrical network
new_concepts.reminder: An electrical network is a graph with positive edge conductances, and it defines a reversible random walk.
new_concepts.definition: An electrical network is a connected, locally finite [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ with a conductance $c(e)>0$ on each edge and resistance $r(e)=1/c(e)$. Its [random walk](c:random-walk) moves from $x$ to a neighbor $y$ with probability $c(x,y)/c(x)$, where $c(x)=\sum_yc(x,y)$, and it is reversible with respect to $\pi(x)=c(x)$. Voltages are functions that are [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) for this walk away from the sources, and the current is $i(x,y)=c(x,y)(v(x)-v(y))$ by Ohm's law.

statement: In a finite [electrical network](c:electrical-network), raising the resistance of edges cannot decrease the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) between two vertices, and adding an edge cannot increase it.

hypotheses.text: $G = (V,E)$ is a finite [connected graph](c:connected-graph), and $a \ne z$ are vertices.
The resistances satisfy $0 < r(e) \le r'(e) < \infty$ on every edge $e$.

conclusion: $R(a \leftrightarrow z; r) \le R(a \leftrightarrow z; r')$, and adding an edge to $G$ does not increase $R(a \leftrightarrow z)$.

proofs.name: Test flow from the other network
proofs.slogan: Use the current flow of the larger resistances as a test flow in Thomson's principle for the smaller ones.
proofs.scope: Both parts: monotonicity in the resistances and the effect of adding an edge.

roles.why: Thomson's principle needs a finite connected network, and adding an edge keeps the graph connected.
The pointwise order of the resistances compares the two energies of the same flow term by term.

steps.slogan: Take the unit current flow of $r'$ as a test [flow](c:flow-network) for $r$.
steps.detail: Unit flows from $a$ to $z$ depend only on the graph. So the unit current flow $i'$ of the network with resistances $r'$ is admissible for $r$, and Thomson's principle gives $R(a \leftrightarrow z; r) \le \sum_e r(e) i'(e)^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two energies of the same flow term by term.
steps.detail: Since $r(e) \le r'(e)$ on every edge, $\sum_e r(e) i'(e)^2 \le \sum_e r'(e) i'(e)^2$, and the right side equals $R(a \leftrightarrow z; r')$ because the current flow attains the minimum in Thomson's principle.

steps.slogan: Extend the current flow of $G$ by zero on a new edge.
steps.detail: The extension keeps the node law and the energy, so it is a unit flow in the larger graph with energy equal to the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) of $G$. Thomson's principle in the larger graph gives the second claim.

steps.slogan: Combine both comparisons into the monotonicity principle.
steps.detail: The comparison of energies gives part (i), and the zero extension gives part (ii). In terms of conductances, the effective conductance is nondecreasing in each edge conductance.

concepts.c:connected-graph: Connectivity makes the effective resistance finite and lets Thomson's principle apply.
concepts.c:flow-network: Unit flows from $a$ to $z$ are the test objects shared by both networks.

statement: On a finite [electrical network](c:electrical-network), the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) between two vertices $a \ne z$ equals the minimum energy $\sum_e r(e)\theta(e)^2$ of a unit [flow](c:flow-network) from $a$ to $z$, and the unit current flow is the unique minimizer.

hypotheses.text: $G = (V, E)$ is a finite [connected graph](c:connected-graph), and each edge carries a conductance $c(x,y) = c(y,x) > 0$ with resistance $r = 1/c$.
The vertices $a$ and $z$ are distinct.

conclusion: With $i$ the unit current flow, every unit flow $\theta$ from $a$ to $z$ satisfies $\mathcal{E}(\theta) = R(a \leftrightarrow z) + \mathcal{E}(\theta - i)$, so $R(a \leftrightarrow z) = \min_\theta \mathcal{E}(\theta)$ and $i$ is the unique minimizer.

proofs.name: Orthogonal decomposition of flows
proofs.slogan: Split any unit flow into the current flow plus a sourceless flow, which is orthogonal to the current in the resistance inner product.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the existence and uniqueness of the voltage and the positivity of the current strength.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the voltage equations a square linear system, connectivity drives the maximum principle, and positive resistances make the energy of a nonzero flow positive.
Distinct terminals give distinct boundary values $W(a) = 1$ and $W(z) = 0$, so the current has positive strength.

steps.slogan: Solve the boundary value problem for the voltage with the discrete maximum principle.
steps.detail: The conditions $W(a)=1$, $W(z)=0$ and [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) at the other vertices form a square linear system. A solution with zero boundary data attains its maximum on $\{a,z\}$, because the maximum spreads to all neighbours of an interior maximum point. So the homogeneous system has only the zero solution, and rank-nullity gives a unique voltage with $0 \le W \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Normalize the current of the voltage into a unit flow with positive strength.
steps.detail: The current $I(x,y) = c(x,y)(W(x)-W(y))$ satisfies the node law off $\{a,z\}$. If its strength were $0$, the value $W = 1$ would spread from the neighbours of $a$ along a path to $z$, which is false. So $i = I/\|I\|$ is a unit flow, and $r\,i = U(x) - U(y)$ with $U(a) - U(z) = R(a \leftrightarrow z)$.

steps.slogan: Sum by parts to pair the potential gradient with an arbitrary antisymmetric edge function.
steps.detail: For every antisymmetric $\theta$, splitting $\tfrac12\sum_{x,y}(U(x)-U(y))\theta(x,y)$ into two sums and renaming the variables in the second gives $\sum_e r(e) i(e) \theta(e) = \sum_x U(x)\,\operatorname{div}\theta(x)$.

steps.slogan: Expand the energy of $\theta = i + \varphi$ and cancel the cross term.
steps.detail: A unit flow has divergence $1$ at $a$ and $-1$ at $z$, so summation by parts gives $\mathcal{E}(i) = U(a) - U(z) = R(a \leftrightarrow z)$. The difference $\varphi = \theta - i$ has zero divergence everywhere, so the cross term $\sum_e r\,i\,\varphi$ vanishes and $\mathcal{E}(\theta) = R(a \leftrightarrow z) + \mathcal{E}(\varphi)$.

steps.slogan: Read off the minimum and its unique minimizer from the energy identity.
steps.detail: Positive resistances give $\mathcal{E}(\varphi) \ge 0$ with equality only for $\varphi = 0$. Hence every unit flow has energy at least $R(a \leftrightarrow z)$, and the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) is attained only by the unit current flow.

new_concepts.reminder: The effective resistance between two vertices is the voltage drop per unit current that flows between them.
new_concepts.definition: In a finite [electrical network](c:electrical-network), let $v$ be the voltage that is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) off $\{a,z\}$ with $v(a)=1$ and $v(z)=0$, and let $\|i\|$ be the strength of the resulting current from $a$ to $z$. The effective resistance is $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(a\leftrightarrow z)=1/\|i\|=1/(c(a)\,\mathbb P_a(\tau_z<\tau_a^+))$. By Thomson's principle, it is also the minimum of the energy $\sum_er(e)\theta(e)^2$ over unit flows $\theta$ from $a$ to $z$.

new_concepts.name: electrical network
new_concepts.reminder: An electrical network is a graph with positive edge conductances, and it defines a reversible random walk.
new_concepts.definition: An electrical network is a connected, locally finite [graph](c:graph) $G=(V,E)$ with a conductance $c(e)>0$ on each edge and resistance $r(e)=1/c(e)$. Its [random walk](c:random-walk) moves from $x$ to a neighbor $y$ with probability $c(x,y)/c(x)$, where $c(x)=\sum_yc(x,y)$, and it is reversible with respect to $\pi(x)=c(x)$. Voltages are functions that are [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) for this walk away from the sources, and the current is $i(x,y)=c(x,y)(v(x)-v(y))$ by Ohm's law.

statement: For the [random walk](c:random-walk) on a finite connected [electrical network](c:electrical-network), the commute time between two vertices $a$ and $b$ equals the total conductance $c_G$ times the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) $R(a \leftrightarrow b)$.

hypotheses.text: $G = (V,E)$ is a finite connected graph with conductances $c(x,y) = c(y,x) > 0$, and the walk has $P(x,y) = c(x,y)/c(x)$.
The vertices $a$ and $b$ are distinct.

conclusion: $\mathbb{E}_a \tau_b + \mathbb{E}_b \tau_a = c_G\, R(a \leftrightarrow b)$ with $c_G = \sum_x c(x) = 2\sum_{e} c(e)$.

proofs.name: Cycle trick and Green function
proofs.slogan: Count the visits to $a$ during one commute cycle in two ways: by stationarity and by the escape probability.
proofs.scope: The whole identity, with the finiteness of hitting times and the uniqueness of the stationary distribution proved along the way.

roles.why: Finiteness and connectivity give finite hitting times and a unique stationary distribution, and the conductances give the stationary weights $c(x)/c_G$.
Distinct vertices make the commute cycle start and end at $a$ only after a visit to $b$, and they define the voltage between $a$ and $b$.

steps.slogan: Bound the hitting times geometrically, so that all expectations are finite.
steps.detail: From every vertex a path of length at most $|V|$ leads to $b$ with probability at least $\delta > 0$, so $\mathbb{P}_x(\tau_b > k|V|) \le (1-\delta)^k$. The strong Markov property at hitting times follows from the Markov property by splitting on the value of the [stopping time](c:stopping-time).

steps.slogan: Identify the escape probability from $a$ through the voltage.
steps.detail: The hitting probability $h(x) = \mathbb{P}_x(\tau_b < \tau_a)$ is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) off $\{a,b\}$, so $1 - h$ is the voltage $W$. One step from $a$ gives $\mathbb{P}_a(\tau_b < \tau_a^+) = \sum_y \tfrac{c(a,y)}{c(a)}(1 - W(y)) = 1/(c(a) R(a \leftrightarrow b))$.

steps.slogan: Count the visits to $a$ before $\tau_b$ as a geometric variable.
steps.detail: After each visit to $a$ the walk escapes to $b$ before returning with probability $p$, so the number $N$ of visits is geometric and the [Green function](c:green-function) value is $\mathbb{E}_a N = 1/p = c(a) R(a \leftrightarrow b)$.

steps.slogan: Build an invariant measure from the visits during one commute cycle.
steps.detail: Let $\tau$ be the first return to $a$ after $\tau_b$ and $\rho(x)$ the mean number of visits to $x$ before $\tau$. Since the cycle starts and ends at $a$, shifting time by one step gives $\rho P = \rho$, and the total mass is $\mathbb{E}_a\tau = \mathbb{E}_a\tau_b + \mathbb{E}_b\tau_a$.

steps.slogan: Show that every invariant row vector is a multiple of the conductance weights.
steps.detail: Functions with $Pf = f$ are constant by the maximum principle on the connected graph, so rank-nullity makes the left kernel of $P - I$ one-dimensional. It contains the [stationary distribution](c:stationary-distribution) $\pi(x) = c(x)/c_G$, so $\rho = (\mathbb{E}_a\tau)\,\pi$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two values of the mean visit count at $a$.
steps.detail: The visits to $a$ before $\tau$ all happen before $\tau_b$, so $\rho(a) = c(a) R(a \leftrightarrow b)$. Also $\rho(a) = \mathbb{E}_a\tau\, c(a)/c_G$. Dividing by $c(a)$ gives the commute time $c_G R(a \leftrightarrow b)$.

concepts.c:random-walk: The walk on the network is the process whose hitting times the identity computes.
concepts.c:electrical-network: The conductances define both the walk and the effective resistance.
concepts.c:effective-resistance: The effective resistance is the network quantity that equals the commute time divided by $c_G$.
concepts.c:stopping-time: Hitting times are stopping times, so the strong Markov property applies at them.
concepts.c:harmonic-function: The hitting probability is harmonic off the two terminals and so equals one minus the voltage.
concepts.c:green-function: The mean number of visits to $a$ before $\tau_b$ is the Green function of the killed walk.
concepts.c:stationary-distribution: The stationary weights $c(x)/c_G$ fix the visit count at $a$ during a cycle.

new_concepts.name: Green function
new_concepts.reminder: The Green function $G(x,y)$ counts the expected visits to $y$ of a random walk from $x$ before it is killed.
new_concepts.definition: For simple [random walk](c:random-walk) $(X_n)$ on $\mathbb Z^d$ and a finite set $\Lambda$, with exit time $\tau=\min\{n\ge0:X_n\notin\Lambda\}$, the Green function is $G_\Lambda(x,y)=\mathbb E_x\big[\sum_{n=0}^{\tau-1}\mathbf 1\{X_n=y\}\big]$. As a matrix, $G_\Lambda=(I-P_\Lambda)^{-1}$, where $P_\Lambda$ is the transition matrix restricted to $\Lambda$, so $G_\Lambda$ inverts the killed [discrete Laplacian](c:discrete-laplace-operator) $-\frac1{2d}\Delta$. For a transient walk one can take $\Lambda=\mathbb Z^d$, and then $G(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge0}P^n(x,y)$.

new_concepts.name: stationary distribution
new_concepts.reminder: A stationary distribution $\pi$ of a Markov chain satisfies $\pi P=\pi$, so a chain started from $\pi$ keeps law $\pi$.
new_concepts.definition: A stationary distribution of a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) $P$ on a state space $S$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\pi$ on $S$ with $\pi P=\pi$, that is, $\int\pi(dx)P(x,A)=\pi(A)$ for every measurable set $A$. On a countable space this reads $\sum_x\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(y)$ for every $y$. If $X_0$ has law $\pi$, then every $X_n$ of the [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) has law $\pi$.

statement: For an irreducible finite [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) with transition matrix $p$ and a root $r$, Wilson's method adds loop-erased runs of the chain one by one. It stops and returns a [spanning tree](c:spanning-tree) rooted at $r$ with $P(T = t) \propto \Psi(t) = \prod_{(x,y) \in t} p(x,y)$. For a connected [electrical network](c:electrical-network), the unoriented tree is the weighted [uniform spanning tree](c:uniform-spanning-tree) with $P(T = t) \propto \prod_{e \in t} c(e)$.

hypotheses.text: $p$ is the transition matrix of an irreducible [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) on a finite state space $V$, and $r \in V$.
The starting states come in any fixed order of $V \setminus \{r\}$, and each run of the chain is independent of the earlier runs.
For the network part, $G$ is a finite connected simple graph with conductances $c(e) > 0$ and $p(x,y) = c(x,y)/\pi(x)$, a reversible [electrical network](c:electrical-network) walk.

conclusion: The method stops with probability 1, and its final [spanning tree](c:spanning-tree) $T$ rooted at $r$ has $P(T = t) = \Psi(t)/\sum_{t'} \Psi(t')$ for every order. For a network, the unoriented tree has $P(T = t) = \Xi(t)/\sum_{t'} \Xi(t')$ with $\Xi(t) = \prod_{e \in t} c(e)$, which is uniform when $c \equiv 1$.

proofs.name: Cycle popping with stacks
proofs.slogan: Drive the chain by stacks of independent moves, show that the popped cycles do not depend on the order, and read the tree law from a product formula.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every finite irreducible chain, every root and every order, and the network part for simple graphs.

roles.why: The stacks use the law $p(x,\cdot)$ at each state, and irreducibility on a finite set makes every run hit the growing tree.
Independent runs have the same law as the stack-driven method, so the order does not change the law of the output.
For the network walk the weight $\Psi(t)$ is $\Xi(t)$ times a factor that does not depend on $t$.

steps.slogan: Put an independent stack of moves under each state except the root.
steps.detail: The entries $S_i^x$ are independent with law $p(x,\cdot)$, and the root has an empty stack. The tops of the stacks give the visible graph, and a visible graph with no [cycle](c:cycle) is a spanning tree rooted at $r$.

steps.slogan: Prove that every order of cycle popping pops the same set of colored cycles.
steps.detail: If a colored [cycle](c:cycle) $C$ is poppable and a different visible cycle $C'$ is popped first, the first cycle of the order for $C$ that meets $C'$ is equal to $C'$. So $C$ stays poppable, and every procedure that stops pops the same set and leaves the same tree.

steps.slogan: Show that Wilson's method run on the stacks pops visible cycles by loop erasure.
steps.detail: The walk follows the tops of the stacks and keeps the loop-erased path. A return to a state on the path closes a visible cycle, which the method pops. The $k$-th departure from a state reads its $k$-th entry, so the walk moves like the [Markov chain](c:markov-chain).

steps.slogan: Show that each run hits the growing tree, so the method stops almost surely.
steps.detail: Each history fixes finitely many entries, and the next entry is fresh, so the stack version has the law of independent runs. Irreducibility gives a uniform chance $\varepsilon > 0$ to hit the tree within $|V|$ steps, so each run ends with probability 1.

steps.slogan: Write the event of popped cycles and final tree as fixed stack entries.
steps.detail: The event that the popped set is $O$ and the tree is $t$ is the event that the stacks show the edges of $O$ and $t$ at their colors. These places are distinct, so the probability is $\Psi(O)\Psi(t)$.

steps.slogan: Factor the law of popped cycles and tree to get tree weights proportional to transition products.
steps.detail: Any set $O$ that can occur can occur with every spanning tree rooted at $r$. So the pairs form a product set, and summing over $O$ gives $P(T = t) = \Psi(t)/\sum_{t'} \Psi(t')$.

steps.slogan: Convert transition products to conductance products for the network random walk.
steps.detail: For $p = c/\pi$, $\Psi(t) = \Xi(t)\,\pi(r)/\prod_x \pi(x)$. Orientation toward $r$ is a bijection from [spanning trees](c:spanning-tree) of $G$ to rooted trees, so the unoriented tree is the weighted [uniform spanning tree](c:uniform-spanning-tree).

concepts.c:markov-chain: The method runs the chain from each new start until it hits the tree.
concepts.c:spanning-tree: The output is a spanning tree, and its law is the subject of the theorem.
concepts.c:electrical-network: Conductances define the reversible walk and the weights of the trees.
concepts.c:uniform-spanning-tree: For a network the output is the weighted uniform spanning tree.
concepts.c:cycle: The proof pops directed cycles of the visible graph of stack tops.

new_concepts.name: uniform spanning tree
new_concepts.reminder: The uniform spanning tree of a finite connected graph is a spanning tree chosen uniformly at random.
new_concepts.definition: The uniform spanning tree of a finite [connected graph](c:connected-graph) $G$ is the random [spanning tree](c:spanning-tree) $T$ with $\mathbb P(T=t)=1/\tau(G)$ for each spanning tree $t$, where $\tau(G)$ is the number of spanning trees. By Kirchhoff's theorem, $\mathbb P(e\in T)$ equals the [effective resistance](c:effective-resistance) between the endpoints of $e$ when all conductances are $1$. Wilson's algorithm samples it with loop-erased random walks.

statement: For a reversible [random walk](c:random-walk) on a countable connected [electrical network](c:electrical-network), the $n$-step [heat kernel](c:heat-kernel) satisfies $p_n(x,y) \le 2\sqrt{\pi(y)/\pi(x)}\,\|P\|_\pi^n\, e^{-d(x,y)^2/(2n)}$, where $d$ is the [graph distance](c:distance-graph-theory).

hypotheses.text: $G = (V,E)$ is a countable connected graph with [graph distance](c:distance-graph-theory) $d$.
The conductances satisfy $c(x,y) = c(y,x) > 0$ on edges with $\pi(x) = \sum_y c(x,y) < \infty$, and $P(x,y) = c(x,y)/\pi(x)$.

conclusion: $p_n(x,y) \le 2\sqrt{\pi(y)/\pi(x)}\,\|P\|_\pi^n \exp(-d(x,y)^2/(2n))$ for all $x, y \in V$ and $n \ge 1$, with $\|P\|_\pi$ the [operator norm](c:operator-norm) on $\ell^2(V,\pi)$.

proofs.name: Chebyshev polynomial expansion
proofs.slogan: Write $P^n$ as an average of Chebyshev polynomials of $P$ weighted by simple random walk on the integers, and drop the low-degree terms.
proofs.scope: The whole bound. A truncation to finite vertex sets replaces the infinite-dimensional spectral theorem.

roles.why: A path from $x$ to $y$ has at least $d(x,y)$ steps, and countability allows the exhaustion by finite sets.
Symmetric conductances make $P$ a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) on $\ell^2(V,\pi)$, and finite $\pi$ makes the unit vectors $f_x$ well defined.

steps.slogan: Show that the transition operator is a self-adjoint contraction of $\ell^2(V,\pi)$.
steps.detail: The form $(f, Pg)_\pi = \sum_{x,y} c(x,y) f(x) g(y)$ is symmetric, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the weights $P(x,\cdot)$ gives $\|Pf\|_\pi \le \|f\|_\pi$. So $P$ is a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) with $0 < \|P\|_\pi \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Compress $P$ to a finite vertex set and express path sums as matrix entries.
steps.detail: For finite $B \ni x, y$, the operator $P_B = 1_B P 1_B$ is self-adjoint on functions supported in $B$ with norm at most $\|P\|_\pi$. Its $n$-th power gives the path sum $p_n^B(x,y) = \sqrt{\pi(y)/\pi(x)}\,(f_x, P_B^n f_y)_\pi$, and $(f_x, P_B^i f_y)_\pi = 0$ for $i < d(x,y)$.

steps.slogan: Expand the power $s^n$ in Chebyshev polynomials with simple random walk weights.
steps.detail: With $s = \cos\theta$ and $w = e^{i\theta}$, the binomial theorem gives $s^n = ((w + w^{-1})/2)^n = \sum_k q_n(k) w^k$, and the real part gives $s^n = \sum_k q_n(k) T_k(s)$ as polynomials. Substituting $S = P_B/\|P\|_\pi$ gives $P_B^n = \|P\|_\pi^n \sum_k q_n(k) T_k(S)$.

steps.slogan: Bound each Chebyshev polynomial of the truncated operator by one in norm.
steps.detail: The self-adjoint operator $S$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues in $[-1,1]$, where $|T_k| \le 1$. So $\|T_k(S)\| \le 1$ in the [operator norm](c:operator-norm).

steps.slogan: Drop the Chebyshev terms of degree below $d(x,y)$ and bound the rest.
steps.detail: Terms with $|k| < d$ vanish because $T_k(S)$ is a combination of powers below $d$. Each other term is at most $q_n(k)$ in absolute value, so $p_n^B(x,y) \le \sqrt{\pi(y)/\pi(x)}\,\|P\|_\pi^n\, P(|S_n| \ge d)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the tail of simple random walk on the integers by a Chernoff estimate.
steps.detail: Markov's inequality for $e^{\lambda S_n}$ and $\cosh \lambda \le e^{\lambda^2/2}$ give $P(S_n \ge d) \le e^{-\lambda d + n\lambda^2/2}$. The choice $\lambda = d/n$ and symmetry give $P(|S_n| \ge d) \le 2e^{-d^2/(2n)}$.

steps.slogan: Let the finite vertex sets exhaust the graph and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: The bound on $p_n^B(x,y)$ does not depend on $B$, and the path sums increase to the [random walk](c:random-walk) transition probability $p_n(x,y)$ as $B$ increases to $V$. Monotone convergence gives the theorem.

$K$ and $L$ are closed [convex sets](c:convex-set) with $K = -K$ and $L = -L$.

proofs.name: Royen's interpolation of the covariance
proofs.slogan: Interpolate the cross-covariance from zero to its true value and show that the box probability of the squared coordinates increases.
proofs.scope: Outline of the whole theorem, after Latała and Matlak. Lemmas 4 to 8 of the source, on Laplace transforms, determinants and gamma-type densities, are cited and not proved here.

roles.why: Gaussian squares have the Laplace transform $|I + \Lambda C|^{-1/2}$, and the interpolated matrices stay covariance matrices.
Closed symmetric convex sets are countable intersections of symmetric strips, which reduces the theorem to coordinate boxes.

steps.slogan: Scale the cross-covariance block by $\tau$ and study the box probability of the squares.
steps.detail: Set $C(\tau)$ with off-diagonal blocks $\tau C_{12}$ and $\tau C_{21}$, and $Z_i(\tau) = X_i(\tau)^2/2$. The theorem for strips is $F(1) \ge F(0)$ for $F(\tau) = P(Z(\tau) \in \prod_i [0, s_i])$, and Lemma 6 lets the derivative pass under the integral.

steps.slogan: Compute the Laplace transform of the density of the squares as a determinant power.
steps.detail: Lemma 4 gives the [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) $|I + \Lambda C(\tau)|^{-1/2}$ of the density $f(\cdot, \tau)$. The [determinant](c:determinant) expands as $1 + \sum_J |C(\tau)_J| \prod_{j \in J} \lambda_j$ over nonempty index sets $J$.

steps.slogan: Show that every principal minor of the interpolated covariance decreases in $\tau$.
steps.detail: The Schur complement gives $|C(\tau)_J| = |C_{J_1}||C_{J_2}| \prod_i (1 - \tau^2 \nu_i)$ with $\nu_i \in [0,1]$. So $a_J = -\partial_\tau |C(\tau)_J| \ge 0$, and the derivative of the transform is a nonnegative combination of $|I + \Lambda C(\tau)|^{-3/2} \prod_{j\in J} \lambda_j$.

steps.slogan: Represent each term as the transform of a mixed derivative of a gamma-type density.
steps.detail: Lemmas 7 and 8 give a density $h_\tau$ on $(0,\infty)^n$, a mixture of products of [gamma distribution](c:gamma-distribution) densities with shapes $3/2 + k$, with transform $|I + \Lambda C(\tau)|^{-3/2}$. The mixed derivative in $x_J$ multiplies the transform by $\prod_{j \in J}\lambda_j$, so $\partial_\tau f = \sum_J \tfrac12 a_J \partial^{J} h_\tau$.

steps.slogan: Integrate each mixed derivative over the box to get a nonnegative boundary integral.
steps.detail: The derivatives of $h_\tau$ vanish as a free variable tends to 0. So the integral of $\partial^J h_\tau$ over the box equals an integral of $h_\tau \ge 0$ on a face, and $F'(\tau) \ge 0$ gives $F(1) \ge F(0)$.

steps.slogan: Pass from coordinate strips to general closed symmetric convex sets.
steps.detail: Hahn-Banach separation writes each closed symmetric [convex set](c:convex-set) as a countable intersection of symmetric strips. Continuity of the [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) along decreasing intersections and a limit $C + \varepsilon I$ give the theorem for every centered Gaussian measure.

concepts.c:gaussian-measure: The inequality compares Gaussian measures of an intersection and of its two parts.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity and symmetry let the proof reduce the sets to intersections of strips.

concepts.c:gamma-distribution: Mixtures of gamma densities represent the derivative of the density of the squares.

statement: For a [stationary sequence](c:stationary-sequence) $(X_n)$ and a set $A$ with $P(X_0 \in A) > 0$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the first return time $T_A$ on $\{X_0 \in A\}$ equals the probability that $A$ is ever visited. So the mean return time to $A$ is $1/P(X_0 \in A)$ when $A$ is visited almost surely.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is a [stationary sequence](c:stationary-sequence): each shift $(X_{k+n})_{n \ge 0}$ has the same law.
The measurable set $A$ satisfies $P(X_0 \in A) > 0$.

conclusion: $\mathbb{E}[T_A \mathbf{1}\{X_0 \in A\}] = P(X_n \in A \text{ for some } n \ge 0)$, so $T_A < \infty$ a.s. on $\{X_0 \in A\}$, and the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) $\mathbb{E}[T_A \mid X_0 \in A]$ equals $1/P(X_0 \in A)$ if $A$ is visited almost surely.

proofs.name: Last visit in a finite window
proofs.slogan: Shift each tail event of the return time to the end of a time window and read it as a last visit to $A$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. No extension of the sequence to negative times is needed.

roles.why: Stationarity moves the event $\{X_0 \in A, X_1 \notin A, \dots, X_{k-1} \notin A\}$ to the end of the window without changing its probability.
A positive probability of $\{X_0 \in A\}$ allows the division that gives the conditional mean.

steps.slogan: Write the mean return time on $\{X_0 \in A\}$ as a series of tail probabilities.
steps.detail: Since $T_A = \sum_{k \ge 1} \mathbf{1}\{T_A \ge k\}$, monotone convergence gives $\mathbb{E}[T_A \mathbf{1}\{X_0 \in A\}] = \sum_{k \ge 1} P(E_k)$ with $E_k = \{X_0 \in A, X_1 \notin A, \dots, X_{k-1} \notin A\}$.

steps.slogan: Shift each tail event to the end of the window $\{0, \dots, K-1\}$ by stationarity.
steps.detail: For $1 \le k \le K$, the vector $(X_{K-k}, \dots, X_{K-1})$ has the law of $(X_0, \dots, X_{k-1})$, so $P(E_k) = P(X_{K-k} \in A, X_j \notin A \text{ for } K-k < j < K)$.

steps.slogan: Decompose the window by the time of the last visit to $A$.
steps.detail: The shifted event says that $K-k$ is the last time in the window at which the sequence is in $A$. These events are disjoint and their union is the event that $A$ is visited in the window, so $\sum_{k=1}^K P(E_k) = P(X_j \in A \text{ for some } j < K)$.

steps.slogan: Let the window grow and divide by $P(X_0 \in A)$.
steps.detail: Both sides increase with $K$, and monotone convergence gives $\mathbb{E}[T_A \mathbf{1}\{X_0 \in A\}] = P(X_n \in A \text{ for some } n \ge 0) \le 1$. A finite [expected value](c:expected-value) forces $T_A < \infty$ a.s., and if $A$ is visited almost surely the division gives $1/P(X_0 \in A)$.

concepts.c:stationary-sequence: Stationarity is the only structural assumption, and it allows the time shift of each tail event.
concepts.c:expected-value: The lemma computes the expected value of the return time on the event $\{X_0 \in A\}$.
concepts.c:conditional-expectation: The mean return time is the conditional expectation of $T_A$ given a start in $A$.

source.ref: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed. (CUP 2019, author's version of January 11, 2019), Theorem 6.3.3, pp. 341-342.
source.note: Durrett decomposes by the last visit before time 0 in a two-sided extension. These steps use the last visit inside a finite window instead and add the identity without the visiting hypothesis.

new_concepts.name: stationary sequence
new_concepts.reminder: A stationary sequence has joint laws that do not change when you shift time.
new_concepts.definition: A sequence $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) is (strictly) stationary when the shifted sequence $(X_{n+k})_{n\ge0}$ has the same law as $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ for every $k\ge0$. Equivalently, every [finite-dimensional distribution](c:finite-dimensional-distribution) is invariant under time shift: $(X_{n_1+k},\dots,X_{n_m+k})$ has the law of $(X_{n_1},\dots,X_{n_m})$ for all indices $n_1,\dots,n_m$ and all $k\ge0$.
